```{python}
       D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 12.5, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="Pin-and-pull toss right vs a wide front")
go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.3), via=[(-0.45, -0.15)])                          # pin the 1 (on the C's backside)
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])                             # pin the 3
go_to(p, "Y", (3.7, 2.9), via=[(-0.2, 4.4)])                               # TE: inside to the Mike
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.0), via=[(-0.3, -3.6)])                            # pin the wide 5
go_to(p, "RG", (0.25, 6.35), "pull", via=[(-1.6, 2.3), (-1.7, 5.4)])       # first puller: kick out the 9
go_to(p, "LG", (4.2, 5.0), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.0), (-2.9, 0.8), (-2.8, 4.6), (0.2, 5.6)])  # second: lead
go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 3.1), "path", speed=4.0)                            # the Mike scrapes ...
go_to(p, "WILL", (5.0, 5.4), "path", speed=4.0, via=[(6.3, 1.4)])          # ... the Will flows over the top
go_to(p, "Z", (5.6, 11.6), via=[(1.0, 12.2)])                              # the corner
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.4, 0.9), "path", speed=4.0)                             # reverse out and toss
go_to(p, "RB", (7.0, 6.2), "run", via=[(-5.6, 2.2), (-3.6, 5.0), (-0.6, 5.6)])
p.pitch("RB", t=0.25)
p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-7.6, 14.0), window=(-8.2, 12.4))
for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT"):
    say(f, p, 2.35, p.players[k].w, "pinned", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, -4.6), (-1.0, -1.6), "empty backside\ngap: both guards\npull", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, 10.0), (-1.7, 5.4), "first puller kicks\nthe end man; second\nleads up inside", color=PURPLE,
         fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (8.6, 2.0), (11.0, 7.0), "SS: unblocked,\nthe back's to beat", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 8.0, -3.6, "wide 5 and 9: too\nwide to reach,\nso pin and pull", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```



The 2024 Washington Commanders, with Kliff Kingsbury calling plays for rookie Jayden Daniels, leaned on pin-and-pull as the
gap-scheme partner to their outside zone; one film breakdown summarized their rule against a front with a 1-technique as
"pull both guards: first guard kicks, second guard leads," which is exactly @fig-pin-and-pull.[^commanders]

## The draw: a run disguised as a pass

The last member of the family barely looks like a run at all. On a [**draw play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw-play)
(or simply a [**draw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw)), the offensive line sets up as if to pass-protect, the quarterback
shows a drop, the pass rushers are allowed to run upfield, and the ball is handed to the back late, after the linebackers have
turned their backs to run to their pass-coverage zones. The rush has *drawn* the defenders out of the play.

```{python}
#| label: fig-draw
#| fig-cap: "A shotgun draw on third-and-11 against a four-man rush (simulated, BDB-format tracking; the yellow line is the line to gain; two safeties are 13 yards deep, above the picture). Watch the two linebackers (orange rings) run away from the ball while the line sets as if to pass. By frame 4 the guards have walled the 3-techniques outside, the center has climbed toward the Will and the Y toward the Mike, and the back (green ring) is through the A gap at linebackers nine yards deep."
def draw_play():
    """A shotgun draw against a four-man rush with the linebackers dropping into zones."""
    off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"),
                    O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DL", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), dl("LT3", "3", -1), dl("RT3", "3", 1), D("RE", "DL", 1.0, 6.0, "E"),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 2.0, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.0, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=11)
    # defense: four rush upfield, the linebackers drop to their zones
    go_to(p, "LE", (-3.6, -5.6), "path", speed=4.6)                    # wide, upfield rushes ...
    go_to(p, "RE", (-3.6, 6.2), "path", speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "LT3", (-1.6, -2.7), "path", speed=2.6)                   # ... and the tackles get walled outside
    go_to(p, "RT3", (-1.6, 2.7), "path", speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (9.5, -3.6), "path", speed=4.4)                   # zone drops, backs to the ball
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (9.5, 3.4), "path", speed=4.4)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (8.6, -1.6), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25)       # ... then react, too late
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (8.6, 1.4), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25)
    go_to(p, "NB", (8.5, -9.5), "path", speed=4.0)
    for k in ("FS", "SS"):
        go_to(p, k, (14.5, p.players[k].w * 1.1), "path", speed=2.0)
    # offense: the line sets as if to pass, then rides the rushers past the ball
    go_to(p, "LT", (-3.0, -4.3), speed=3.0, via=[(-1.8, -3.9)])        # kick slide, ride him deep
    go_to(p, "RT", (-3.0, 4.4), speed=3.0, via=[(-1.8, 3.9)])
    go_to(p, "LG", (-2.0, -1.9), speed=2.2, via=[(-1.6, -1.6)])        # set, then turn the 3 out
    go_to(p, "RG", (-2.0, 1.9), speed=2.2, via=[(-1.6, 1.6)])
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.4, 0.0), speed=2.0)                              # sets, nobody comes ...
    go_to(p, "C", (7.5, -0.9), speed=5.0, delay=0.3)                   # ... so he climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "Y", (7.9, 2.2), speed=4.2, via=[(1.5, 4.6)])             # releases, then blocks the Mike
    for k in ("X", "Z", "H"):
        p.route(k, [(0, 0), (13, 0)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, 0.2), "path", speed=3.0)                     # sells the drop
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.5, 0.9), "run", speed=1.5)                      # steps up as if to protect
    go_to(p, "RB", (8.0, -0.4), "run", speed=6.2, delay=0.55, via=[(-5.9, 0.55), (-2.0, 0.2), (1.5, 0.0)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.95)
    return p


animation_or_strip(draw_play(), [0.0, 0.8, 1.45, 2.45], lateral=(-8.6, 8.6), window=(-7.4, 11.6), ncols=2,
                   width_in=5.4,
                   notes=["3rd and 11: four rushers, two LBs, two deep", "pass set; LBs turn and run to their zones",
                          "handoff behind the rushers' backs", "guards wall off the tackles; through the A gap"],
                   rings=(("RB", style.THIRD), ("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)))
```

The draw belongs in a gap chapter because it is built on the same principle as the trap: **let the defender go where he wants
to go, then block him there**. The guards in @fig-draw do not try to stop the 3-techniques from rushing; they let them come
upfield and then turn them outward, away from the A gaps. The tackles ride the ends wide and deep, the way they would on any
pass. The more eagerly the defense rushes the passer, the bigger the hole in the middle gets. And the linebackers, who on a
normal run would be the problem, have spent the first second running *away* from the ball to cover receivers.

That tells you when to expect it: on **passing downs, against a four-man rush with linebackers who drop**. Third-and-long is the
classic draw situation, and a defense with two deep safeties and two linebackers dropping into zones is the classic draw
defense.

Be honest about what it buys, though, because you have the tools from
[Downs, Distance and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd). A six-yard gain on
third-and-11 is a *failed* play by [success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate): the offense punts anyway.
In the 2023–2025 regular seasons, NFL designed runs on third-and-10 to -12 converted about 12% of the time and averaged
about −0.29 [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) a play; dropbacks in the same spot converted about 27% and averaged
about −0.11.[^thirdlong] Some of that gap is selection (offenses that have already given up on the down, late in a half or
protecting a lead, call runs), but the point stands: a third-and-long draw is usually a deliberate *conservative* choice.
Coaches call it to avoid a sack or an interception, to shorten the punt or set up a field-goal try, and to make the
pass rush hesitate a half-step on the next third down. Against a defense that drops its linebackers it is also, now and
then, a long run. It is rarely the best way to get eleven yards.

The trade: the draw is helpless against *interior* pressure. If a linebacker comes *forward* at the snap instead of
dropping, or walks up into an A gap before the snap, he is standing exactly where the play needs to go, and nobody is
assigned to him because the line is busy pretending to pass-block. A defense that sits a linebacker in the middle as a
[spy](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd) on a running quarterback ruins it for the same reason. Pressure
off the edge is a different story: an outside blitzer runs himself past the play, which is exactly what the draw wants.

Paul Brown's Browns made the draw famous in the late 1940s with Marion Motley, a fullback of about 232 to 238 pounds who could
also pass-block, which made the fake believable. One story says it began by accident, with Otto Graham improvising a handoff
on a broken pass play; another has Brown already experimenting with a delayed handoff to Motley in 1945. Either way it was a
Cleveland staple by the time the Browns joined the NFL in 1950.[^draw] Its descendants, the
quarterback draw and the run-pass option, belong to [Option Football](03-04-option-football.qmd) and
[RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd).

## The family on one page

Every play in this chapter answers the same two questions, *where do the extra blockers come from, and who is left
free?*, and each carries a rule the line can apply to whatever front it sees. @tbl-family puts them side by side, with
the holes in [03-01](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)'s gap letters. To draw any of these plays against a new front, start
from its rule column, not from a remembered picture.

| Play | Where it hits | The line's rule | Extra blockers | Left free |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Power | off-tackle: the C gap, or the D gap outside a tight end | gap, down, backer on the play side; center blocks back | backside guard leads; fullback or H-back kicks out | the backside end |
| Counter | off-tackle, like power | the same play-side rules; center blocks back | backside guard kicks out; tackle (or H-back) leads | the backside end, unless a tight end or H-back fills |
| Duo | A or B gap, decided by the Mike | doubles on both tackles, everyone else man-on; the doubles own the linebackers | none | nobody in a six-man box; the extra man in a bigger one |
| Trap | B gap, just inside the trapped tackle | let one lineman through; the man in front of him releases inside to a linebacker | backside guard, on a short pull | nobody, if the trap lands |
| Wham | like trap | like trap, but the guards climb | a tight end or H-back crossing | like trap |
| Iso | a bubble: an open gap with a linebacker behind it | block the man on you; the uncovered lineman takes the backside linebacker | fullback leads onto the play-side linebacker | the safeties |
| Sweep, pin-and-pull | outside the end man | pin the man in your backside gap, or pull if it is empty | both guards | usually a safety, and the backside chase |
| Draw | A gaps | pass set; wall the rushers away from the middle; center and tight end climb | none: the rushers take themselves out | any linebacker who does not drop |

: The gap family on one page. {#tbl-family}

## Gap or zone? How coaches choose

Almost every NFL team runs both families, so the real question is when each one is the better call. Five things push a coach
one way or the other.

**The front.** Gap schemes need *angles*, so they like fronts that give them: a 3-technique to block down on, a 1-technique to
block back on, an end man who can be kicked out. They are vulnerable to movement, since a defender who slants into the space a
puller is running through can blow up two blockers at once. Zone, built to absorb movement, is the natural answer to slanting
fronts. Wide fronts, as you saw, push teams toward pin-and-pull and kick-outs; a penetrating 3-technique invites the trap or the
wham; linebackers who flow fast to stop outside zone invite counter. Defenses know this too, and some fronts are built partly
to take the angles away: a lineman on a blocker's *inside* shoulder (a 4i on the tackle, say) leaves that blocker no down
block to make, and if he penetrates he is standing in the lane the pullers run through.
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) shows those fronts.

**The defense's shell.** Against a light box (two deep safeties, six in the box), the offense already has its hats and wants
movement: duo and inside zone. Against a seven-man box, power and counter win the point of attack by moving hats there. Against
eight, even they leave a defender free (the backside end *and* the safety who came down), which is when offenses read one of them
with the quarterback ([Option Football](03-04-option-football.qmd)) or stop running and throw, which is the point of loading the box.

**The personnel.** Power wants a kick-out blocker: a fullback, an H-back, a second tight end. Iso needs a fullback. Wham needs a
tight end who can trap. A team with no fullback on the roster runs a different gap game from one that has an All-Pro at the
position.

**The offensive line.** Zone wants linemen who can move laterally and stay on their feet, and has made a home for lighter, quicker
linemen. Gap schemes want linemen who can drive a man off the ball on a down block and guards (or tackles) who can pull and hit on
the move. Teams draft and coach their line for the run game they want, and their run game also bends toward the line they have.

**The situation and the sequence.** Short yardage favours the known hole and the extra hat of a gap scheme. Long yardage favours
the draw. And every run sets up another: counter exists because power exists, the trap because 3-techniques penetrate, the
bootleg because the backside end chases ([Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)
is the full version of that idea).

| | Gap schemes | Zone schemes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Blockers are assigned... | men and gaps, before the snap | areas, by rule after the snap |
| The hole is... | chosen in advance (it can move a yard: kick or log) | wherever the wall cracks |
| Extra blockers come from... | pullers, fullbacks, tight ends moved across | double teams; a quarterback who reads the backside end |
| The back's job | follow the puller, read one block | press the aiming point, read the defense |
| Beats... | big, static fronts; seven-man boxes (moves hats to the hole); aggressive penetrators (trap) | slants and stunts; fast-flowing linebackers (cutback) |
| Struggles against... | movement into the pullers' path; defenders who read the guards | penetration; wide fronts (outside zone) |
| Tell on the broadcast | a lineman pulls | the whole line steps the same way |

: Gap and zone, side by side. {#tbl-gap-zone}

In 2019 Kyle Shanahan, the most famous wide-zone coach in football, surprised people by adding more power and counter to his
49ers' run game; he told his team he had called such plays only about seven times in more than a decade as a play-caller.[^shanahan] That is the modern consensus in one
decision: a scheme is a menu, not an identity.

How do the two families compare league-wide? The public numbers come from charting services, since play-by-play data does not
record the blocking scheme. Pro Football Focus's charting had inside and outside zone together making up nearly half of all NFL
running plays in 2022, with draws only about 3%. Over 2020–2022 it had power averaging 4.53 yards a carry, inside zone 3.90,
counter 3.90, outside zone 3.78 and duo 3.71 (and draws, called against defenses set for a pass, 5.95).[^pffconcepts] Treat
those as rough. Yards per carry is a crude measure, and each play is called in the situations it suits: duo against light
boxes on early downs, power in short yardage, the draw on third-and-long. No family dominates, which is why almost every team
runs both. The Go Deeper box at the end shows how to count the concepts yourself in tracking data.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In the game, "HB Power" is a play in the menu that either works or doesn't, and the defense picks a play without seeing yours.
In a real NFL game the line coach has decided during the week which gap runs fit this opponent's front, the play-caller
sequences them so that each one sets up the next (power, then counter off the same look; trap after the 3-technique has been
penetrating all half), and the linemen still adjust after the snap: the center makes a call on the front, the puller decides
kick or log, the back decides which side of a double team to take. There is no best run, only a best run *against this* on *this* down.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2019"}
**The season:** the Ravens ran for 3,296 yards, breaking the NFL single-season team record the 1978 Patriots had held for 41
years, and Lamar Jackson ran for 1,206 of them.[^ravens2019] Coordinator Greg Roman's menu mixed nearly every play in this
chapter (power, counter, trap and wham, pin-and-pull) with outside zone and Jackson's option reads, often from formations with an
extra tight end or fullback Patrick Ricard, and used motion and a changing mix of personnel groups to keep defenses from
settling into the right numbers.[^roman]

**What to notice:** the quarterback is part of the blocking arithmetic. On a Ravens power play, the end left unblocked on the
backside is often *read* by Jackson instead of ignored, so he cannot chase the back without giving Jackson the edge. That is
the gap scheme's price (the free backside defender) being paid by the option, which is the subject of the next chapter. The
full case study is [The Ravens' Lamar Jackson Run Game](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024"}
**The season:** Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards in 16 games, the ninth 2,000-yard season in NFL history, and the Eagles beat
Kansas City 40–22 in Super Bowl LIX. A *Philadelphia Inquirer* film study that November described an offense that alternated
zone and gap runs "noticeably," using gap-scheme changeups with pulling linemen to balance its zone game, behind a line coached
by Jeff Stoutland.[^eagles24]

**What to notice:** this is the team to practise the zone-or-gap call on. Pick one Eagles drive and, before every run, guess zone
or gap from the formation; then, on the snap, check your guess against the line: does everyone step the same way, or does
somebody pull? Keep score. Because the Eagles alternated the two families from the same looks, a good score means you are
reading the line, not the formation. The full case study is
[The Eagles: Trenches and the Tush Push](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd).
:::

## Spotting a puller before the snap

Because a puller runs to the hole, finding him early is the single most useful habit in watching gap runs. Defenses know this too:
many linebackers are taught to read the guards, and a pulling guard is their signal to run with him. So both sides are looking
for the same tells, and offenses work to hide them.

**Before the snap**, look for:

- **The backfield, and which guard to watch.** The guard to watch is the *backside* one, the guard away from where the play
  is likely to go, so first guess the direction. In the shotgun, gap runs, like zone runs, usually send the back across the
  quarterback's face, so a back offset to the left usually runs right, and the backside guard is the one on the *same* side
  as the back (in @fig-counter, the back is offset left and the left guard pulls). Under center, a fullback or H-back offset
  to one side is often the kick-out man, and power usually goes *toward* him, so watch the guard away from him. With nothing
  to go on (an I-formation, a back directly behind the quarterback), watch both guards: on the high end-zone replay they are
  side by side, and the one that moves first tells you. A back set deeper than usual needs time, which counter and the sweep
  require (the pullers have to get there first).
- **The guards' stance.** A lineman about to pull often has less weight on his hand, his feet a little more staggered, his hips
  ready to turn. This is the [heavy hand](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) tell in reverse: a puller is
  going *sideways*, not forward, and many give it away with a light hand or a slight cheat backward off the ball, since depth
  gives him room to clear his teammates' heels. The best pullers hide it, and some offenses deliberately line up their guards the
  same way on every snap.
- **The formation and the tendency.** Certain personnel groups and formations are gap-heavy for every team (two tight ends with
  one off the ball, the I-formation, an H-back on the wing); the broadcast graphics and your
  [prediction log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) will teach you which.

**At the snap**, the first step settles it. A pulling lineman's first step is backward and sideways, opening his hips toward
the play (the bucket step; some coaches call it a drop step); a zone lineman's first step is sideways and forward; a
pass-blocking lineman's first step is straight back with his shoulders still square to the defense. One look at the
backside guard tells you which. One exception to keep in mind: on dart (@fig-dart) the guard stays home and the *tackle*
pulls, so if the guard blocks but the run still looks like power, check the backside tackle.

Offenses exploit the defenders who read guards. A pulling guard on a play-action pass pulls linebackers toward the fake, and a
"false pull" on a run sends them the wrong way; counter itself is a lie told with the back's first step. Those plays exist
precisely *because* the tell is so reliable. Trust the guard, but notice when the offense is using your trust against you.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Follow the guard.** For one quarter, on every run, watch the *backside* guard instead of the ball. In the shotgun that is
usually the guard on the same side as the offset back; under center, the guard away from an offset fullback; if you cannot
tell, watch both and see which one moves.

*Before the snap*

- Count the box and find the extra blockers: a fullback, an H-back, a second tight end. Where would a kick-out come from?
- Check the guards' stance and depth. Is one a little off the ball, weight back?

*The first half-second*

- **Does a guard pull?** If yes, call "gap" and say the direction out loud: the play is going where he is going.
- **Does a second blocker pull with him?** Two pullers *with the back stepping away first* means counter. Two guards pulling wide
  with the back flowing the same way means a sweep or pin-and-pull. Any pull with the back stepping the other way means counter.
- **The guard blocks, but the backside tackle pulls?** Dart: power with a tackle as the puller.
- **Nobody pulls, but the line fires straight ahead in double teams?** Duo. **The whole line steps the same way?** Zone.
- **A defensive tackle comes through untouched?** Look for the trap (a guard) or the wham (a tight end) arriving at his hip.
- **The line drops back as if to pass, and the back gets the ball late?** Draw.

*After the play (on the replay)*

- Find the kick-out. Did the kick-out man kick the end out or log him in, and did the back go to the side of his helmet?
- Find the free defender: on power, the backside end. Did he make the tackle?

In your [prediction log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), add one letter after each run: **G** (gap) with
the play's name if you can (P, C, D, T, W, I, S for power, counter, duo, trap, wham, iso, sweep) or **Z** (zone). After a quarter,
look at how often the guard told you the truth.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. One puller: which play?** Second-and-7, shotgun, the back offset to the right. @fig-drill-1 shows the first
half-second. One guard is pulling. Is this power, counter or trap? Say which defender the offense is letting through on
purpose, who will block him, and where the back will run.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: the first half-second (shotgun, the back offset right). Look at the left side of the defensive line."
off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.8, "R")]
dfn = [dl("PE", "5", -1), dl("DT", "3", -1), dl("NT", "1", +1), dl("BE", "5", +1),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, -1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 2.4, "W"),
       D("FS", "FS", 11.0, -5.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 5.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7, title="Drill 1: one puller. Which play?")
go_to(p, "LG", (1.3, -1.0), via=[(-0.1, -1.2)])                   # releases inside, past the 3
go_to(p, "C", (0.3, 0.45), via=[(-0.45, 0.15)])                   # back block on the 1
go_to(p, "RT", (1.3, 2.3), via=[(-0.1, 2.7)])                     # releases inside
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.1), via=[(-0.3, -3.6)])                   # the 5
go_to(p, "Y", (0.35, 4.35), via=[(-0.3, 4.75)])                   # down on the end
go_to(p, "RG", (-2.3, -0.9), "path", via=[(-1.6, 1.3), (-2.3, 0.4)])   # pulls left, flat and short
go_to(p, "DT", (-1.0, -2.4), "path", speed=3.0)                   # nobody touches him
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.3, 0.2), "run", via=[(-4.8, 1.2)])             # across the quarterback's face
p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-7.6, 7.6), window=(-7.0, 12.8))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Trap left.** The 3-technique on the left is being let through on purpose: the left guard in front of him has released
*inside* him, toward the Mike, without touching him, and nobody else is coming at him from the front. The right guard's
pull is the giveaway that he will be trapped: it is short and flat, aimed at the space behind the center, not a long run
to the edge. The guard will hit the 3 from the inside, where he is not looking, and the back will cut just inside the
trap block, through the B gap on the left, with the left guard and right tackle already climbing to the two linebackers.

How to rule out the others: on **power** the 3 would get a down block (here nobody touches him), and a fullback or H-back
would be heading for the edge to kick out the end man (nobody is). On **counter** the back would step *away* from the play
first and two blockers would pull; here the back goes straight across the quarterback's face, to the left, and only one
guard pulls. The one thing that beats this call is a disciplined 3-technique who reads the guard's inside release and
squeezes down into the hole before the trapper arrives.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Third-and-long.** Third-and-11 from midfield. The offense is in the shotgun with three receivers and a tight end
split out; the defense shows a dime package (six defensive backs) with two deep safeties, four linemen in wide alignments, and one
linebacker seven yards deep (@fig-drill-2). The offense is going to hand the ball off. Which run from this chapter has the best
chance, and what would ruin it?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: third-and-11 (yellow line). Shotgun, the back beside the quarterback, the tight end (Y) in the slot; a dime defense with four rushers aligned wide, one linebacker (M) about seven yards deep, and two safeties 14 yards deep."
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DL", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), dl("LT3", "3", -1), dl("RT3", "3", 1), D("RE", "DL", 1.0, 5.6, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.0, 0.5, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.0, "NB"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.0, "DB"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 14.0, 8.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=11, title="Drill 2: 3rd and 11. Which run?")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-17.6, 17.6), window=(-7.6, 16.6))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The draw.** Everything in the picture is a draw invitation. The defense has five men in the box against five offensive
linemen, the rushers are lined up wide so they can get to the quarterback, and the only linebacker will drop into a zone
at the snap. If the line sets up to pass, the wide ends will rush upfield and outside, the 3-techniques will rush through the
B gaps, and the middle of the field, the A gaps, will be empty except for the linebacker, who will be backpedalling. Hand the
ball off late, after the rush has committed, and the back is running at a linebacker who is turned the wrong way and safeties 14
yards deep.

Why not duo, which this chapter called a two-high play against light boxes? Because duo needs the linebacker to *fill*: the
back reads him and the double teams come off onto him. On third-and-11 this linebacker will be running backward at the
snap, and a play built to catch a man running away from it is the draw.

Will it get 11 yards? Probably not, and the offense knows it: as the draw section showed, third-and-long runs rarely convert
and usually lose expected points. A draw here is a conservative call (no sack, no interception, a shorter punt) and a
warning shot to the pass rush.

**What would ruin it:** the linebacker coming *forward* at the snap, a blitz up the middle, or a "spy" assigned to sit in the
middle and watch the back. Any defender who stays home in the A gaps is standing exactly where the draw needs to go, and nobody
is assigned to block him.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Two pullers, one decision.** Counter right. @fig-drill-3 freezes the play as the two pullers arrive: the left
guard, whose job is the end man, and the left tackle behind him, who was going to turn up inside the kick-out. The end has
crashed hard inside as the right tackle blocked down, and the Mike is scraping outside. What should the guard do, what
should the tackle behind him do, where should the back go, and who is left for the back to beat?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the moment of decision on counter right. The right tackle has blocked down on the 3; the end (5) has crashed inside behind him from his alignment (dashed square); the pulling left guard and left tackle (purple rings) and the back are arriving. The right guard is climbing to the Will. Outside, the Mike is scraping and the strong safety (SS) is coming down."
off = [O("RG", "RG", -0.7, 1.6, "RG"), O("RT", "RT", -0.7, 3.2, "RT"), O("LG", "LG", -1.6, -0.6, "LG"),
       O("LT", "LT", -2.9, -2.4, "LT"), O("RB", "RB", -4.8, -0.6, "R")]
dfn = [dl("DT", "3", 1), D("PE", "DL", 0.45, 4.35, "5"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 0.2, "W"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 2.8, "M"), D("SS", "SS", 7.0, 9.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: two pullers, one decision")
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, 0.6), via=[(-0.2, 1.6)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 5.6), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "SS", (4.4, 8.0), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "LG", (-1.7, 3.0), "path", via=[(-1.9, 1.4)])
go_to(p, "LT", (-2.8, 1.0), "path", via=[(-3.0, -0.4)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 1.4), "run")
p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("LT", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=4.8, lateral=(-4.4, 12.4), window=(-7.0, 9.6))
ghost(f, p, (1.2, 5.2), (0.8, 4.85))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Log him and bounce, and the tackle follows the log outside.** The end has taken away the inside: there is no room to
kick him out, because he is already standing where the hole was supposed to be, and the guard cannot get his head inside
him. So the guard takes his *outside* shoulder, gets his head and body outside him and seals him in (a log block). The
pulling tackle, who was going to turn up inside the kick-out, now has no inside to turn up into, so he follows the log
outside and takes the first defender to show, usually the Mike scraping over the top. The back, reading the guard's
helmet, bounces outside the log behind the tackle.

The defender left over is the **strong safety**, coming down outside, and he is the back's to beat. That is not an
accident: a defense that tells its end to spill the ball outside is counting on a fast defender outside to meet it there,
the alley player ([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) explains
who that is and why). The offense's counter-move is to block that man, often with a wide receiver's crack block (a receiver
cutting back inside to block a defender from the side, which
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) covers).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **A gap scheme blocks men, not areas, and aims at a hole chosen in advance.** The core gap run is down blocks (the inside
  wall), a kick-out (the outside wall) and a puller through the middle; the rest of the family drops or swaps one part. The
  hole moves only as far as the end man forces it, and the back runs to the side of the kick-out man's helmet (kick or log).
- **Power is the template.** Block down, kick out with the fullback, lead with the backside guard, hinge the backside, and leave
  the backside end unblocked. It turns a play side of three blockers against four defenders into five against four, with the
  spare man doubling the 3 and then climbing. It does not add a blocker to the box; it moves one.
- **The rest of the family varies one thing.** Counter changes the back's first step and pulls two (guard kicks, tackle wraps).
  Duo pulls nobody and drives two double teams into a light box. Trap and wham leave a lineman unblocked and hit him from the
  side, with a guard or a tight end. Iso sends a fullback at one linebacker. Pin-and-pull and the sweep take the same blocks
  outside. The draw blocks the rush where it wants to go.
- **Every gap run names who is left free.** Usually it is a defender far from the hole (the backside end); the offense bets he
  arrives late, or reads him with the quarterback.
- **Coaches choose by front, shell, personnel and line.** Gap schemes like angles, seven-man boxes and big static fronts; zone
  likes movement; duo and zone like light boxes; most teams run both from the same looks. The rules travel from front to front,
  which is why a backside 3-technique turns power into dart.
- **Follow the guard.** A puller runs to the hole. Find the backside guard on every run (in the shotgun, usually the one on the
  back's side), and you will call the direction of most gap plays before the back gets there.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Finding gap runs in real tracking data.** The play diagrams and both animations here are gridiron simulations written in NFL
Big Data Bowl coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) labels every run with PFF's primary run
concept, so you can count how often each concept was called (the first `print` below), pull every power or counter play, find the pulling guard by his first-second movement, and draw the real
version of @fig-counter. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code (in the web edition, under "Show the Python") is not
run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
print(plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].value_counts().head(12))      # how often each concept was called

counters = plays[plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].astype(str).str.upper().str.contains("COUNTER")]
g, pl = counters.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)

# the puller is the offensive lineman who moves farthest sideways in the first second after the snap.
# BDB tracking has no position column, so take the linemen from players.csv first.
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")
linemen = set(players.loc[players["position"].isin(["T", "G", "C"]), "nflId"])
snap = one[one["frameType"] == "SNAP"]["frameId"].min()
ol = one[one["nflId"].isin(linemen) & one["frameId"].between(snap, snap + 10)]
print(ol.groupby("displayName")["y"].agg(lambda s: abs(s.iloc[-1] - s.iloc[0])).sort_values().tail(2))
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.6, 1.3, 2.3])                    # the same moments as the simulated counter
```
:::

[^gdb]: "Gap, down, backer" (sometimes "gap, down, linebacker" or "GDL") is the standard play-side rule for power and counter in
    coaching manuals and clinic talks. One coaching write-up states it as: gap, "if there is somebody in your immediate backside
    gap, block them"; down, "if there is somebody over or inside shoulder of the linemen in your backside gap, block them"; backer,
    "if there is nobody in the gap or down, head to the linebacker": Chris Haddad, "How To Install Gap Scheme Runs Into Your
    Offense," Viqtory Sports, <https://www.viqtorysports.com/the-gap-scheme-how-its-run-in-every-offense/>. For power's
    assignments in general, see Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015).

[^trey]: "Counter run," Wikipedia (Washington's counter trey of the 1980s and early 1990s, "modeled from the Nebraska
    Cornhuskers"; the left guard and left tackle pull while the right side blocks down; the back steps left, then takes the ball
    right): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter_run>. Gibbs on Nebraska ("We saw some film on Nebraska, and Tom Osborne was doing
    some really innovative things with his line up front.... So, we stole it."), and Nebraska's counter dated to 1982: Dave Feit,
    "Greatest Huskers by the Numbers: 6," Sports Illustrated (All Huskers),
    <https://www.si.com/college/nebraska/football/dave-feit-s-greatest-huskers-by-the-numbers-6-keith-jones-darin-erstad-tom-osborne-national-champions>.
    The counter trey as "the Redskins' signature running play that Gibbs implemented his first season," with Grimm and Jacoby
    pulling: Associated Press, "Gibbs expected to use same bag of tricks" (2004), <https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna5946857>; Rick
    Gosselin, "State Your Case: Joe Jacoby": <https://rickgosselin.com/state-your-case-joe-jacoby/>. Jersey numbers (Grimm 68,
    Jacoby 66): Pro Football Hall of Fame, <https://www.profootballhof.com/players/russ-grimm/>; Hogs Haven, "Redskins by the
    (Jersey) Numbers: #66 - Joe Jacoby," <https://www.hogshaven.com/2017/8/9/16105032/redskins-by-the-jersey-numbers-66-joe-jacoby>.
    Washington's 14–2 record in 1983: "1983 Washington Redskins season," Wikipedia,

[^titans]: Henry's 2020 season ("a league-high 378 times for a league-high 2,027 yards and a league-high 17 touchdowns"): CBS Sports,

    along the interior," the line working "directly upfield"), Arthur Smith's system from 2019, and the Titans leading the league

    ("His forte was the trap play"): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Motley>.

[^wham]: Chris B. Brown, "Draw It Up: The 49ers and the 'Wham' Play," Grantland (Oct 17, 2011): the wham is "similar to a traditional
    trap play, except the trap block comes from the H-back, not a guard," and is "a surprisingly simple block":
    <https://grantland.com/the-triangle/draw-it-up-the-49ers-and-the-wham-play/>.

[^wham-sf]: Same Grantland column (the 49ers' 25–19 win at Detroit on Oct 16, 2011, Week 6; the plan to leave Ndamukong Suh

[^personnel]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play and participation data (`load_participation`), 2025 regular
    season, pass and run plays with a down: 10.3% of 32,813 plays had two or more running backs and fullbacks on the field (21
    personnel alone was 7.0%). Reproduced in [nflverse in Python](../13-analytics-and-data/13-01-nflverse-in-python.qmd).

[^sweep]: "Sweep (American football)," Wikipedia (the Packers sweep; Kramer and Thurston pulling; Hornung and Taylor; "an offense

    Thurston a guardian angel on famous power sweep": <https://www.packers.com/news/fuzzy-thurston-a-guardian-angel-on-famous-power-sweep>.
    Vince Lombardi with W. C. Heinz, *Run to Daylight!* (Prentice-Hall, 1963).

[^pinpull]: The covered/uncovered pin-and-pull rule ("If there is a defender in their gap they are going to block down on this defender.
    If there is not a defender ... they are going to pull"): Youth Football Online, "Simple Rules for the Pin and Pull Play":
    <https://youthfootballonline.com/simple-rules-for-the-pin-and-pull-play>; Chris Haddad, "How To Install The Pin & Pull Play,"
    Viqtory Sports (covered linemen "gap block in the back-side gap," uncovered linemen "pull to the play-side"):
    <https://www.viqtorysports.com/pin-pull-what-is-it-and-how-is-it-run/>.

[^commanders]: Alert the Post, "Cutup Friday: 2024 Commanders Pin Pull RPO's" (May 16, 2025): "Pin Pull is a gap compliment for
    Outside Zone"; "Against Over fronts with a 1-technique nose, the Commanders will pull both guards most of the time. First guard
    kicks, second guard leads": <https://alertthepost.substack.com/p/cutup-friday-2024-commanders-pin>. Kingsbury was the
    Commanders' offensive coordinator in 2024; for 2026 he is the Rams' assistant head coach (planning/FACTS-current.md §9).

[^draw]: "Draw play," Wikipedia (the botched pass play on which Otto Graham improvised a handoff to Motley, after which Brown "began
    to work it in as a regular play"): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draw_play>; "Marion Motley," Wikipedia (at Great Lakes in
    1945, "Brown's experimentation with a new play: a delayed handoff later called the draw play"; "listed at 238 pounds"):
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Motley>; Pro Football Hall of Fame biography (6-1, 232 pounds):
    <https://www.profootballhof.com/players/marion-motley/biography/>.

[^dart]: Jonny Page, "Eagles Concepts: Dart," Bleeding Green Nation (Jul 21, 2023): dart "is a gap scheme run, that looks a lot
    like one-back power but with a pulling tackle instead of a pulling guard," also called "one-back power or tackle power"; it
    "allows your interior lineman to stay inside," protecting against "quick interior penetration from the opposing defensive
    tackle," but "the tackle has further to travel so he needs to be very athletic":
    <https://www.bleedinggreennation.com/2023/7/21/23790118/eagles-concepts-dart>.

[^counternames]: Counter is "named after who is pulling. For example, GH Counter (the guard and H-back pull) is essentially the same
    as GT Counter (the guard and tackle pull)": Jonny Page, "Eagles Film Room: Concept of the Week - GH Counter," Bleeding Green
    Nation (Sep 21, 2024), <https://www.bleedinggreennation.com/2024/9/21/24249061/eagles-film-room-concept-of-the-week-gh-counter>.
    Counter trey, GT counter and counter as names for the same guard-and-tackle play, and leading an H-back instead so teams can
    "keep the backside tackle in to block": Chris Haddad, "How To Install The Counter Play," Viqtory Sports,
    <https://www.viqtorysports.com/how-to-run-counter-in-football-complete-guide/>.

[^pffconcepts]: Jonathon Macri, "Fantasy Football: Finding an edge in offensive run concepts," PFF (May 19, 2023): inside and
    outside zone "accounted for nearly 50% of all running plays in the league" in 2022; draws were "3.04% of rushing plays" in
    2022; three-year (2020–2022) yards per carry of 4.53 (power), 3.90 (inside zone), 3.90 (counter), 3.78 (outside zone),
    3.71 (duo) and 5.95 (draw): <https://www.pff.com/news/fantasy-football-finding-an-edge-in-offensive-run-concepts-2023>.

[^thirdlong]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`load_pbp`), 2023–2025 regular seasons, third down with 10 to
    12 yards to go, run and pass plays: 162 designed runs (runs that were not quarterback scrambles) converted 12.3% and averaged
    −0.29 EPA; 2,748 dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles) converted 26.6% and averaged −0.11 EPA. "Converted" uses nflverse's
    `first_down` flag.
